notes:
I've gathered notes on all 21 verses, though the detail falls off from verse 18 onward. I didn't find any real split between Protestant traditions on this chapter. I also found nothing on it from ligonier.org, thegospelcoalition.org, spurgeon.org, desiringgod.org, gty.org, the Lutheran sites, the Pentecostal sites (apart from Enduring Word) or oca.org. My searches turned up no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on 2 Kings 11.

A note on sources: on biblehub, Gill's comments sit on the same pages as the others, but I never got his text clearly enough to quote him. Some biblehub pages mix several commentators without clear labels; I name a commentator only where the page does.

**1. The traditional reading, verse by verse**

**v. 1**
- Ahaziah had been killed by Jehu (2 Kings 9:27-29). Athaliah used his death to take power herself. Ahaziah was executed by Jehu, as recorded in 2 Kings 9:27-29. She used the occasion of her son's death to take power for herself — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Guzik reads the killings partly as revenge: Jehu had completely destroyed all of Ahab's descendants in Israel. Now, after Jehu's coup, Athaliah tried to save something for Ahab's family by trying to eliminate the house of David in Judah. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Ellicott says "the seed royal" means all who might set up claims to the succession. Earlier attacks had already removed Ahaziah's brothers and kinsmen, so those whom Athaliah slew would be for the most part Ahaziah's own sons — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary explains her motive. Once Ahaziah died she would have lost the post of queen mother (*gebirah*), which would have passed to the widow of Ahaziah, the mother of the new sovereign — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- Precept Austin and Constable both see Satan trying to wipe out the line of the Messiah. Precept Austin compares Pharaoh and Herod (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-11-commentary). Constable quotes another writer who calls it one of the many attempts Satan made to exterminate the male offspring to make the coming One, the promised Savior, the seed of the woman, impossible. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-11.html
- Precept Austin also cites John Walton: wiping out a previous dynasty was common in the ancient Near East. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-11-commentary

**v. 2**
- Jehosheba was probably Ahaziah's half-sister by another mother. Ellicott (citing Josephus) adds that Athaliah would not have allowed her daughter to marry the high priest of Jehovah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The "bedroom" was most likely a storeroom for bedding, not a sleeping room. Ellicott describes the room in the palace where the mattresses and the coverlets were kept, and says the baby was later moved secretly into the temple grounds. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests the queen's servants may not have searched very hard. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- Guzik: Through her courage and ingenuity, she preserved the royal line of David through which the Messiah would come. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Biblehub's study notes compare Jehosheba's courage to that of Moses' mother. — https://biblehub.com/2_kings/11.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott thinks Joash lived in priests' rooms, perhaps in the high priest's own house within the temple grounds. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says six years of Athaliah meant Baal worship was winning in Judah and the temple fell into disrepair. It also thinks a party loyal to the LORD kept her somewhat in check. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- Guzik: For the sake of David, God remembered His promise and spared this one young survivor — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Precept Austin quotes Dale Ralph Davis: the chapter never says "the LORD did" anything. It shows God working in a hidden, roundabout way. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-11-commentary

**v. 4**
- On "the seventh year," Ellicott suggests this may be when perhaps discontent at Athaliah's tyranny had reached a climax. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary identifies the Carites with David's Cherethites, possibly Carian mercenaries. It notes that Jehoiada had no authority to summon the officers; he must have invited them secretly. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- Guzik on showing them the boy: one reason Athaliah lasted six years was that no one knew any alternative. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Precept Austin's point is that Jehoiada secured loyalty first and only then revealed the king. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-11-commentary
- Ellicott compares Chronicles, which gives the priests and Levites a bigger part. He says Kings is the older account and the chronicler drew his information from a large historical compilation somewhat later than the Books of Kings — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm

**vv. 5–7**
- Ellicott: there were two places to hold, the palace (to watch Athaliah) and the temple (to protect the heir). He notes that that the Sabbath was the day on which they relieved each other is known only from this passage — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary's version: the guard had five companies. Three held the palace while two guarded the king in the temple. The aim was to secure the palace without stopping the queen from leaving it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- Both commentators say the "gate of Sur" (called "Foundation Gate" in Chronicles) can't be identified with certainty. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html

**v. 8**
- The guards formed two lines so the king could walk safely, and anyone forcing through was to be killed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that nobody tried, and adds that boys are restless, so the guard had to move with him. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html

**v. 9**
- The Pulpit Commentary: here the army put itself entirely under the priest's orders. "The priest" here means the high priest. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: The arms which David had laid up in the Temple as spoils of war were now to be used, appropriately enough, for the restoration of David's heir to the throne. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- Guzik makes the same point. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Keil and Delitzsch (as quoted on biblehub) say the weapons were handed out because the men had come unarmed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/11-11.htm

**v. 11**
- The altar is the altar of burnt offering in the outer court. The guard was drawn up across the court from wall to wall. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html

**v. 12**
- **The Testimony.** Wesley calls it the book of the law, given to remind the king of his duty under Deuteronomy 17:18. He explains that the law is called a testimony because it is a witness of God's will, and man's duty. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_kings/11.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks a copy of the Law, perhaps the Ten Commandments, was laid on the boy's head. This showed that he would rule under the law, not by whim. It calls the ceremony probably new, a sign of royal power being limited. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- Precept Austin: the king's authority is limited by God's Word. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-11-commentary
- **The anointing.** The Pulpit Commentary notes this is the first royal anointing mentioned in Judah since Solomon. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- **Guzik's six steps.** He reads the scene as a pattern: revealed, crowned, given the Word, received, anointed, praised. He applies it to how believers receive Christ. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/

**vv. 13–14**
- Precept Austin points to irony: the Baal-worshipping queen enters the house she had despised. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-11-commentary
- **"By the pillar."** The Pulpit Commentary reads this as "on the platform," a raised royal stand in front of the sanctuary. The "officers" were the guard captains; trumpets were usual at coronations. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
- **"Treason!"** Guzik calls it a well-founded and godly treason against a tyrannical, wicked ruler. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Constable says the real traitor was Athaliah, who was not of David's line. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-11.html

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik calls the order both righteous and prudent. He says Jehoiada cared about keeping the temple from being defiled. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Ellicott: she was led to the royal stables beside the palace and killed there. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- Wesley takes "the army" (KJV "host") in v. 15 to mean companies of Levites. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_kings/11.htm
- Guzik quotes Patterson and Austel, who compare her death to her mother Jezebel's. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/

**v. 17**
- **The covenant with the LORD.** The Pulpit Commentary says the apostasy of Jehoram, Ahaziah and Athaliah was regarded as having put an end to the old covenant, and therefore it was solemnly remade or renewed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/11-17.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch call it a renewal of the covenant of Moses (Exodus 24), based on the Testimony. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/11-17.htm
- **The covenant between king and people.** Wesley calls it a civil covenant. The king promised to rule justly, and the people to defend and obey him. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_kings/11.htm
- Guzik draws a wider principle: neither king nor citizens have absolute rights over or against the other. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/

**v. 18**
- Guzik: Jehu had torn down Baal's temple in Samaria; now the temple of Baal in Jerusalem was destroyed, and appropriately destroyed by the people of the land. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- Guzik links the people's anger to sacred objects taken from the LORD's temple for Baal (2 Chronicles 24:7). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-11/
- The Pulpit Commentary calls a Baal temple in Jerusalem a deliberate insult to the LORD. It reads the posting of guards as restoring temple worship: true worship replaced false. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html

**vv. 19–20**
- Ellicott: the "Gate of the Guards" was probably the main entrance to the palace enclosure. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the people rejoiced because, with Athaliah's death, the accursed house of Ahab ceased and David's house was back on Judah's throne. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-kings-11.html

**v. 21**
- Precept Austin: a seven-year-old king shows that this was God's doing. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-11-commentary
- Constable: Joash reigned 40 years (835–796 BC). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-11.html

**2. Where Protestant traditions differ**

These are differences of emphasis, not open disagreements.

- **v. 1, why it happened.** Wesley (Methodist) and the Geneva Bible (Reformed) both say the massacre was God's judgment on Jehoshaphat for marrying his son into Ahab's house. Wesley: this dreadful judgment God permitted upon him and his, to shew how much he abhors all such affinities. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_kings/11.htm. The Geneva note says God used the cruelty of this woman to destroy the family of Ahab. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_kings/11-1.htm
- **v. 2, marriage.** Wesley draws a lesson about marrying children to wise and good people. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/2_kings/11.htm
- **vv. 4–16, was the revolt right?** Everyone I read approves of it, but they justify it differently:
  - The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican authors) insists Jehoiada was no mere revolutionary and would have agreed with St. Paul that "the powers that be are ordained of God." It argues that treason against a government itself born of treason was not a crime, but might be the highest duty. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-kings-11.html
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel) calls it "godly treason" and applies it to rebelling against Satan. — https://enduringword.com/time-for-treason/
- **The priests.** Farrar's *Expositor's Bible* is unusually critical of the priesthood as a class, though mostly when discussing Joash's later reign. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/2_kings/11.htm

**3. Other views**

- **Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):**
  - The text never actually says Athaliah worshipped Baal or built Baal's temple; only Josephus claims this, centuries later. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/athaliah/
  - The writer suggests she may have worshipped the LORD, which would make the plotters' motives more political than religious. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/athaliah/
  - The writer adds that the story skips over Joash being her grandson, and so part-foreign and a usurper himself. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/athaliah/
- **Older critics.** Ellicott records Thenius doubting that Jehosheba was the high priest's wife; Ellicott himself trusts Chronicles. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_kings/11.htm
- **Catholic.**
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on Jerusalem says Joash was proclaimed king at age six and Athaliah "was stoned to death." That doesn't match the text, where she is killed by the sword (vv. 16, 20). — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08344a.htm
  - The Knox translation on newadvent renders v. 4 as the temple being "witness of their oath," and gives Joash and Jehoiada their Vulgate names, Joas and Joiada. — https://www.newadvent.org/bible/2ki011.htm
